question: On the summit of Mount Everest, does water boil at a higher or a lower temperature than at sea level?
source_excerpt: Water boils at lower temperatures at higher altitudes

extra.why_interesting: Most people know water boils at 100°C and assume that is fixed. On Everest's summit it boils at roughly 70°C, which is why mountaineers struggle to cook pasta or brew a proper cup of tea.
extra.verification_notes: Lower atmospheric pressure at Everest's summit lowers water's boiling point to about 70°C versus 100°C at sea level; this is a physical constant and cannot go stale.

explanation: Water boils at around 70°C on Everest's summit. Air pressure there is only about a third of the pressure at sea level, so water molecules escape as vapour more easily. Your tea would never get properly hot, and pasta takes far longer to cook.

question: How long does sunlight take to travel from the Sun to your face?
source_excerpt: sunlight takes 8 minutes and 10 to 27 seconds to reach Earth, depending on the time of year.

extra.why_interesting: When you look at the Sun, you are seeing it as it was several minutes ago. The three options span very different scales.
extra.verification_notes: Sunlight takes about 8 min 10-27 s to reach Earth depending on season, so '8 minutes' is correct and the distractors are clearly wrong (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light).

explanation: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to cover the roughly 150 million kilometres to Earth. If the Sun suddenly vanished, we would keep seeing it shine for over 8 minutes.

question: Natural gas has no smell at all, so suppliers add a pungent sulfur compound to make leaks detectable. Name this family of foul-smelling chemicals.
source_excerpt: Methanethiol, commonly known as methyl mercaptan, is added to natural gas as an odorant, usually in mixtures containing methane.

extra.why_interesting: The 'gas smell' everyone recognises does not come from the gas at all. It is a sulfur compound added on purpose as a safety warning.
extra.verification_notes: Natural gas odorants are mainly thiols (mercaptans) such as tert-butylthiol, isopropyl and methyl mercaptan; THT is a minor non-thiol sulfide but the answer stays standard.

explanation: Mercaptans, also called thiols, are added in tiny amounts. Common examples are tert-butyl mercaptan in natural gas and ethyl mercaptan in propane. They smell like rotten eggs or cabbage, and the human nose can detect them at concentrations of a few parts per billion. That is what makes a gas leak noticeable.

question: Name the gas that makes bread dough rise and also puts the fizz in soft drinks.
source_excerpt: Carbonated water... is plain water into which carbon dioxide gas has been dissolved. Most soft drinks have carbonated water as a base.

extra.why_interesting: It links two everyday things that seem unrelated: fluffy bread and fizzy drinks. The same gas causes both.
extra.verification_notes: CO2 is the gas from yeast/leavening in dough and is dissolved to carbonate soft drinks; no contradicting or newer information found (https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbonated_water).

explanation: Yeast feeds on sugars in dough and releases carbon dioxide, which forms the air pockets in bread. Soft drinks are carbonated by dissolving carbon dioxide under pressure. When you open the bottle, the gas escapes as bubbles. The same gas is what we breathe out.

question: A lightning bolt heats the air around it for a split second. Compared with the surface of the Sun, is that air roughly half as hot, about the same temperature, or about five times hotter?
source_excerpt: Energy from a lightning channel heats the air briefly to around 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, much hotter than the surface of the sun.

extra.why_interesting: Most people think of the Sun as the ultimate 'hot thing'. Learning that an ordinary thunderstorm briefly produces something several times hotter than the Sun's surface is a genuine 'no way!' moment.
extra.verification_notes: NOAA NSSL and Britannica give ~50,000°F (~30,000 K) for lightning-heated air, about 5x the Sun's ~10,000°F surface; no newer developments contradict this.

explanation: A lightning channel can briefly reach around 30,000 °C. The visible surface of the Sun is only about 5,500 °C. This sudden, extreme heating makes the air expand explosively, and that explosion is the thunder you hear.

question: Two spoons, one metal and one wooden, have sat in the same drawer all night, so both are at room temperature. Why does the metal one feel colder when you pick it up?
alternative_answers: It draws heat from your hand faster
Metal takes heat from your skin quicker
source_excerpt: Metal, in contrast, carries heat away quickly. Metal is a good conductor of heat.

generation_metadata.reasoning_pattern: Pattern 10: The Lateral Thinking Puzzle (everyday physics variant)

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has noticed that metal feels colder than wood. Few realise both objects are at exactly the same temperature, and that their hand is really sensing how fast heat leaves it.
extra.verification_notes: Standard physics: metal's high thermal conductivity draws heat from the hand faster than wood, so it feels colder at the same temperature; the more precise property is thermal effusivity, but the answer is acceptable.

explanation: Both spoons really are the same temperature. Metal is a far better conductor of heat than wood, so it draws warmth out of your skin much more quickly. Your nerves sense that rapid heat loss as 'cold'. Wood is an insulator, so it barely pulls heat from your hand and feels warmer.
